Subject: Before the launch sprint starts
Hi Gurpreet,
Thanks for putting me on the app launch. I'm genuinely excited about it, and I want to flag a few things now rather than in week three.
I work best when I've slept. So I'll be offline from 9 pm to 8 am, and the work chat will be off on my phone then. If something is truly urgent, please call; I'll pick up.
I'll take a proper lunch away from my desk, and I walk for twenty minutes after it. That walk is where half my bug fixes come from, honestly.
In the last two weeks before launch I'm happy to stretch to longer days, as long as the weekend after is fully off.
On the last project I said yes to everything, and by the end I was making mistakes I'd never normally make. I'd rather give you my best eight hours than my worst fourteen.
Let me know if any of this clashes with the plan. Happy to talk it through.
Arohi

qa.q: When will Arohi be offline?
qa.a: From 9 pm to 8 am, with the work chat off.

qa.q: How does Arohi feel about the new project, and what worry sits behind the email?
qa.a: Arohi is genuinely excited but also wary, remembering how saying yes to everything on the last project led to unusual mistakes.

qa.q: Why is sending this before the sprint a wise move?
qa.a: Stating limits early lets Gurpreet plan around them, instead of Arohi quietly wearing out and raising it in week three.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet read this email?
qa.a: Gurpreet might be surprised at first, but can see a clear offer to stretch before launch and a way to reach Arohi for real emergencies.

grounding: Shows a worker protecting sleep, meals, movement and time off, and stating limits early before a demanding project.

subtype: Reducing load rather than powering through [Response]
passage:
Jatin, you asked how I got through last spring without falling apart. Honestly, I nearly didn't. I, Binita, was running the school's exam timetable, coaching the debate team and covering a colleague's two classes. By March I had headaches every afternoon and was snapping at the children.
My first instinct was to push harder. Wake earlier, stay later. Instead, one Friday I wrote a list of everything I was doing and took it to my principal. I said, "I can do the timetable and my own classes well. I can't do all of this well." I asked if the debate team could go to Mr Pinto till May, and if the extra classes could be split.
She said yes to both. I was shocked. I'd expected her to think I wasn't committed.
The headaches didn't stop straight away, so I saw my doctor the next week too. By May I was sleeping again, and teaching properly.

qa.q: What did Binita take to the principal?
qa.a: A list of everything Binita was doing.

qa.q: Why was Binita shocked when the principal said yes?
qa.a: Binita had been afraid the principal would see the request as a lack of commitment, so the quick yes came as a relieved surprise.

qa.q: What made Binita's request effective?
qa.a: Binita brought a clear list, named what could be done well, and proposed specific changes: debate to Mr Pinto till May and the extra classes split.

qa.q: What might the principal have thought on seeing the list?
qa.a: The principal probably saw a teacher being honest about limits early, and judged that sharing the work was better than losing Binita's good teaching.

grounding: Shows a worn-down person asking to drop or share tasks and seeing a doctor when symptoms continue, instead of pushing harder.

passage:
Saturday.
Told Naveen Sir today I'm not coming to swimming anymore. Said it's boring. Same lanes, same whistle, same chlorine smell.
It wasn't boring in the first month. I loved the kicking drills, and I was faster than the two others from my class. Then this week he started us on butterfly stroke. I swallowed half the pool. The little kids in the next lane laughed. My shoulders ached all evening.
Naveen Sir said, "Everyone looks like a drowning cat for the first three weeks. Give it till the end of the month." I said I've got too much homework.
It's the same as keyboard last year. I stopped when we reached chords with both hands. And badminton, when the smashes started.
Maybe I'm just someone who gets bored. Or maybe I leave right when it gets hard. I don't really want to think about which.
Hafsa

qa.q: Which stroke did Naveen Sir start this week?
qa.a: Butterfly stroke.

qa.q: What was Hafsa really feeling when calling swimming boring?
qa.a: Hafsa seems embarrassed and discouraged after swallowing water, aching shoulders and being laughed at, and "boring" covers that discomfort.

qa.q: What could Hafsa try before deciding to stop?
qa.a: Hafsa could take Naveen Sir's offer, stay till the end of the month, and decide once the first hard weeks are over.

qa.q: How might Naveen Sir see Hafsa leaving now?
qa.a: He likely sees a swimmer quitting just before the stroke gets easier, which is why he says everyone looks like a drowning cat for the first three weeks.

grounding: Shows a teenager dropping an activity as soon as it gets difficult and calling it boredom, a pattern repeated before.

passage:
In the career cell at his engineering college, Arnab sat across from Minakshi ma'am, the counsellor, with his marksheet folded into a small square.
"You've failed two mechanical papers this year," she said gently. "And last time you told me you spend every evening at the photography club."
"Yes, but I've done five semesters. Five. If I switch now, all of that goes to waste."
"What would the next three semesters look like if you stay?"
He unfolded the marksheet and folded it again. "More of this. Probably more backlogs."
"And the photography? The college magazine picked your pictures twice."
"That's just a hobby."
"Is it? Try this: forget the five semesters for a minute. If you were starting today, which would you choose?"
Arnab was quiet for a long time. The fan ticked overhead.
"Not mechanical," he finally said, and looked almost frightened by his own voice.

qa.q: How many semesters has Arnab done?
qa.a: Five semesters.

qa.q: What does Arnab folding and unfolding the marksheet suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Arnab feels anxious and torn, stuck between the five semesters already spent and a future he doesn't want.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi's question about starting today help?
qa.a: It set the past effort aside and made Arnab judge only what the coming years would bring, which is what should decide.

qa.q: How might Minakshi see Arnab calling photography "just a hobby"?
qa.a: Minakshi seems to doubt it, pointing out that the magazine picked the pictures twice and asking, "Is it?"

grounding: Shows a student staying on a course that no longer fits because of the semesters already invested.

passage:
Monday, 3 June. Anand slammed the German textbook shut in the hostel common room. Four months of classes, and he still froze whenever the teacher asked anything out loud. "I'm done. I'm dropping it," he told Joseph.
Joseph didn't argue. "Before you drop it: is it the goal you don't want, or the way you're learning?"
Friday, 7 June. Anand sat with a notebook and made three columns. Goal: the master's in Aachen, still yes. Method: grammar drills alone every night, no speaking; that was the problem. Phase: exam week, sleeping badly. He decided to join a weekend speaking circle, drop half the drills, and take one week off after exams. On the last page he wrote, "Review: 15 July. If I still hate it, I stop."
Monday, 15 July. Anand ordered coffee in German at the speaking circle and got the right cup. He opened the notebook, read the review line, and wrote: "Continue."

qa.q: What review date did Anand set?
qa.a: 15 July.

qa.q: How was Anand feeling on 3 June?
qa.a: Anand felt frustrated and defeated, still freezing whenever asked to speak after four months, and wanted to drop German.

qa.q: What did Joseph's question help Anand do?
qa.a: It helped Anand separate the goal from the method and the phase, so he changed how he learned and set a review date instead of quitting on a bad day.

qa.q: What would change if Joseph had simply agreed that Anand should drop it?
qa.a: Anand might have given up the master's plan because of a poor method and a hard exam week, not because the goal was wrong.

grounding: Shows a person asking whether the goal, the method or a passing phase is the problem, adjusting and setting a review date before quitting.

passage:
12 August. Nilesh sat in his car outside the bank branch where he'd worked for three years and typed a resignation letter he didn't send. His father had cried with pride when he got this job. His manager, Kavitha, had just trusted him with the new loans desk. He felt sick at the thought of telling either of them, and strangely light at the thought of doing it.
2 September. Nilesh told his parents at dinner that he had an offer from a small design studio. His father put his spoon down. "A bank job is security." Nilesh went through the reasons he'd written down: work he actually wanted, a salary he could live on, savings to cover a few months. His mother said, "Give him time."
3 September. He asked Kavitha for ten minutes. "I'm leaving at the end of the month. I'll finish the loans desk set-up and write everything down for whoever comes next." Kavitha sighed, then nodded. "Thank you for telling me early."

qa.q: What did Nilesh tell Kavitha he would do before leaving?
qa.a: Finish the loans desk set-up and write everything down for whoever comes next.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Nilesh have in the car on 12 August?
qa.a: Nilesh felt guilty and sick about letting down his father and Kavitha, and at the same time strangely light, relieved at the thought of going.

qa.q: Which parts of how Nilesh left will protect his reputation?
qa.a: Telling Kavitha early, offering to finish the set-up, and writing everything down for the next person.

qa.q: Why might Nilesh's father react to the news as he did?
qa.a: His father sees the bank job as security and was deeply proud of it, so leaving it feels like a risk.

grounding: Shows a young professional deciding to leave a job with mixed guilt, fear and relief, weighing family expectations and handing over carefully.

passage:
Career counselling notes. Client: Pema, 24. Session 3, with parents.
Pema has finished two years of accountancy training and wants to switch to a one-year teaching course. In session 2 she told me she had tried raising it at home by shouting, "It's my life," and her father walked out.
Today her parents came. Her mother held her handbag on her lap the whole time. Her father spoke first: "Two years gone. What if teaching also doesn't work? Then what?" He seemed less angry than scared; his hands were shaking.
Pema stayed calm. She showed them one page: the course fees she has saved, three schools she has already visited, and a promise to finish her current exam in May so the accountancy door stays open.
Her father read the page twice. He didn't agree, but he asked, "Which school did you like best?"
Next steps: one more joint session in two weeks. I've told Pema that a question is a start.
Usha

qa.q: What did Pema promise to finish in May?
qa.a: Her current exam, so the accountancy door stays open.

qa.q: What was Pema's father feeling in the session?
qa.a: He seemed more scared than angry, hands shaking, worried that two years were gone and teaching might not work either.

qa.q: Why did Pema's approach in session 3 work better than shouting?
qa.a: Pema stayed calm and brought one page with saved fees, schools visited and a back-up plan, which answered her father's fear instead of fighting it.

qa.q: How does Usha read the father's question about the school?
qa.a: Usha sees it as a start, a sign he is beginning to engage even without agreeing.

grounding: Shows a person changing career meeting a parent's fear of failure, and a calm plan reaching the parents better than defiance.

passage:
Mina had worked at Priscila's bakery in São Paulo for two years when a hotel kitchen offered her a pastry job. She told Priscila first, before anyone else, on a quiet Tuesday morning while the ovens warmed.
"I've taken a new job. I wanted you to hear it from me."
Priscila wiped her hands slowly. "When?"
"I'll give you four weeks. And I'll still do the Oliveira wedding cake on the twentieth, since I promised them."
For the next month Mina trained the new baker, Leandro, on the sourdough starter and wrote the feeding times on the fridge door. When a customer asked why she was leaving, she said only, "A new challenge. I've learned so much here." She never mentioned the broken mixer or the late payslips.
On her last day Priscila handed her a jar of the starter. "Come back and bake for us whenever you like."

qa.q: What did Mina promise to still do before leaving?
qa.a: The Oliveira wedding cake on the twentieth.

qa.q: What might Priscila have felt when Mina gave the news?
qa.a: Priscila was probably disappointed and a little shaken, wiping her hands slowly, but later grateful enough to hand over a jar of the starter.

qa.q: Which of Mina's choices kept the bridge open?
qa.a: Telling Priscila first and in person, giving four weeks, finishing the wedding cake, training Leandro, and not complaining to customers.

qa.q: How might Leandro experience Mina's last month?
qa.a: Leandro got real training on the starter and the feeding times on the fridge door, so Leandro can take over without guessing.

grounding: Shows a person leaving a job honestly, finishing promised work and leaving without blame.

"Naveen, please. Just send me photos of your practical file. Just this once."
"It's due at eight tomorrow, Preeti. You said you'd started."
"I had tuition, then the maths test, then Mummy's cousin came over... I've done two experiments out of ten."
"Everyone copies the practical file anyway."
"Exactly! So it's not a big deal."
Naveen hesitated, then sent the photos. "Change the readings a bit at least."
At one in the morning Preeti was writing "the solution turned pale pink" for an experiment she had never seen. She paused. Last term she had copied the physics file too, and in the viva she couldn't explain a single diagram.
"Ma'am will ask questions in the viva," she typed.
"Then just learn my answers," Naveen replied.
Preeti looked at the page, then at the empty titration columns. She kept copying, but slowly, and her stomach stayed tight the whole time.

qa.q: How many experiments had Preeti done?
qa.a: Two experiments out of ten.

qa.q: What does Preeti's tight stomach suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Preeti feels guilty and uneasy, remembering the viva where she couldn't explain the copied physics file, even while telling herself it is just this once.

qa.q: What could Preeti do instead of copying tonight?
qa.a: Preeti could write up the two experiments honestly and tell the teacher in the morning that the rest is late, asking for a short extension.

qa.q: What is it like for Naveen when Preeti keeps asking?
qa.a: Naveen seems torn, hesitating before sending the photos and then trying to limit it with "Change the readings a bit at least."

grounding: Shows a teenager copying work under deadline pressure, telling themselves it is just this once while their own ability slips.

subtype: Cutting corners in a group task [Actor]
passage:
Dear Elizabeth,
Something has been sitting on my chest since Thursday, and you're the only one far enough away to tell.
Our group presented the water survey project. Ravi did the whole analysis, the charts, the regression, everything, but he was down with fever and missed the presentation. I presented his section. When Dr Menon asked who built the model, I said, "We worked on it together," and she looked straight at me and said, "Excellent work, Sangeeta." I just said thank you.
Everyone does this, right? Group marks are group marks. Ravi won't even know. That's what I keep telling myself at night, and it works for about ten minutes.
Except the individual marks count towards the grade. And Ravi is applying for the research assistant post, and Dr Menon is the one choosing.
I think I have to write to her. I've opened the email four times.
Love,
Sangeeta

qa.q: Who did the analysis for the project?
qa.a: Ravi did the whole analysis, the charts, the regression, everything.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta feel, despite the "everyone does this" excuse?
qa.a: Only briefly: Sangeeta still feels guilty, with something sitting on the chest, and the excuse works for about ten minutes.

qa.q: What should Sangeeta write to Dr Menon?
qa.a: A short, honest email saying Ravi built the model and did the analysis, so the individual marks and the research post credit the right person.

qa.q: How might Ravi be affected if Sangeeta says nothing?
qa.a: Ravi could lose individual marks and a fair chance at the research assistant post, since Dr Menon believes Sangeeta did the work.

grounding: Shows a student letting a teammate's uncredited work pass as their own and using everyone-does-it to soften the guilt.
